ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the figure is the AC power supply port, and the supply voltage is labeled \(\dot U\). In the upper line, a resistor \(R_1\) is connected in series, and the voltage across its two ends is labeled \(\dot U_1\). After \(R_1\), the circuit divides into two parallel branches: the middle branch is \(R_2\) connected in series with the inductive reactance \(X_{L2}\), and the voltage across this parallel load is labeled \(\dot U_2\); the right branch is the inductive reactance \(X_{L1}\) connected in series with the capacitive reactance \(X_C\). Reasoning: According to the figure, the circuit can be equivalent to \(R_1\) in series with a parallel load, where the impedance of one branch is \(Z_2=R_2+jX_{L2}=2+j2\), and the impedance of the other branch is \(Z_3=j(X_{L1}-X_C)=j(4-X_C)\). The problem gives \(\dot U_1=\dot U_2=\frac{1}{2}\dot U\), indicating that the voltage drops on the series \(R_1\) and the parallel load are equal phasors; the series current is the same, so the equivalent impedance of the parallel load must be equal to \(R_1\), and it is purely real. The admittance of the parallel load is \(Y=\frac{1}{2+j2}+\frac{1}{j(4-X_C)}\). First calculate \(\frac{1}{2+j2}=\frac{2-j2}{8}=\frac14-j\frac14\). The admittance of the right branch \(\frac{1}{j(4-X_C)}\) is purely imaginary. To make the equivalent impedance of the load real, the imaginary part of the equivalent admittance should also be zero, that is, the imaginary part of the right branch cancels \(-\frac14\). At this time, the real part of the admittance comes only from the middle branch, \(\Re(Y)=\frac14\,\text{S}\), so the equivalent impedance of the parallel load is \(Z_{eq}=1/Y=4\,\Omega\). Because \(Z_{eq}=R_1\), therefore \(R_1=4\,\Omega\).

method.method_draft: From the image, model the circuit as R1 in series with a parallel load consisting of Z2=R2+jXL2 and Z3=j(XL1-XC). From the text, substitute R2=2 Ω, XL2=2 Ω, XL1=4 Ω, and U1=U2=U/2 as phasor equality. Since U1 and U2 are equal phasor drops in series, the parallel-load equivalent impedance must equal R1 and therefore be real. Compute the load admittance Y=1/(2+j2)+1/[j(4-XC)]. Force the imaginary part of Y to be zero to make the load equivalent real; this gives the needed reactive cancellation. Then the real part of Y is 1/4 S, so the load equivalent is 4 Ω, hence R1=4 Ω.

method.method_draft: From the image, take U2 as the reference voltage across the two shunt branches. Because the text says U1=U2 as phasors and R1 is a resistor, the current through R1, I=U1/R1=U2/R1, must be in phase with U2. The right branch, made only of XL1 and XC in series, supplies only a ±90° reactive current; it can be chosen to cancel the -jU2/4 reactive component so that the total current is in phase, but it contributes no in-phase component.
